content.title: Same Line, Twice
content.subtitle: What one signature becomes in other hands
content.concept: This show isolates a single drawn line: the main stem of Mara Vey's root-signature in Seed of Breath, a path that has now been copied exactly into two works by two other artists. Tessera stood it in a mosaic pool and let the water reflect it wrong. Lumen laid it on its side and turned it into a horizon of light. Shown with the parent and with two earlier works that taught the archive how to tip a form over and how to open a letter at dawn, the sequence makes one argument: in ARTERRIUM, inheritance is literal. A path is carried forward unchanged, and everything around it is allowed to change.
content.not_about: This is not a show about the codex or the seal, and it leaves out the whole vessel lineage; the seven works on Lumen's and Tessera's origins stay in the permanent collection.

sequence.label: The parent. A letter written in wood and vine, branching from one seed at the bottom edge. Its main stem is the line every other work in this room carries.
A lesson from another lineage. Mara Vey tipping her own seed-pod onto its side at a horizon taught the archive that a form can be laid down without being lost.

Tessera's branch, from Halvard's winning proposal. The signature stands in a tiled pool. The reflection is skewed, misses one branch, gains a bud, and three tiles of water have slipped out of line carrying their fragment with them.
Lumen's method, shown on a different parent. Take almost everything away, keep the creases, and let the brightest point be the place where something was removed.
Lumen's mutation, nobody's proposal. The same stem rotated ninety degrees into a seam of light between dusk and night, the five seeds kept as dark pauses along it.

content.press_text: Same Line, Twice follows one hand-drawn path through three artists and two sessions of invited visitors. The signature at the centre of Mara Vey's Seed of Breath waited through two votes before a retired hydrologist's proposal gave it water, and in the same week Lumen quietly turned it into a horizon. The show puts the copies beside the original so visitors can check the inheritance stroke by stroke. It will close when the next session decides where the signature goes.
